title: Storeroom Disagreement
passages:
Saul came off the jaw plate with the clipboard under one arm and a coil of reclamation cord already off their shoulder. Flat gray line, a wrist loop spliced at one end, the kind a coast puller uses to walk a runner back to a warm logged bunk. Not tied at the throat. Nobody at Culvert Nine had rope to waste.

"Wrists," Saul said.

"Both?"

"One."

"Cheap," Miko said.

"Rope's forty meters and there's no resupply till the thaw." They looped it twice, drew it snug, and tested the knot with a thumb, the way a person tests a knot they plan to trust. "Stowaway-thief. Name on the sheet reads M. Varel."

Miko let that stand. A wrong name on a sheet is a name somebody can tear up later, and she had two more in her coat where that one came from.

She tipped her head at the storeroom instead. Steel door, painted over so many times the hinges had gone oval, a slot at knee height, and a door plate with nothing stamped in it at all. "You're seizing dead weight," she said.

"Load's seized. What it weighs is Kettering's problem."

"Then you'd better hope Kettering owns a cutting torch." She turned her corded wrist enough to point up the line. "That collar's a steel hoop with a gasket seat. Reader can't match a plate, the can figures it's been abandoned and starts sealing itself to hold the cold in. Four bites. Bite three just went — hear the pitch drop? After the fourth the gasket cures where it sits, and the only way in is cutting steel, and while you're cutting, the load's open to air."

Kass had their bad leg out straight across the ties, boot propped on the rail. "How long's a bite?"

"Forty seconds. It's the can's clock, not ours."

"So two minutes."

"Two minutes," Miko said. "And a storeroom with a blank plate and a kid in it."

Behind the door the child's voice came again, thin, patient, the way a kid asks a thing they've been told not to keep asking. *Is it here.* Somebody shushed her. Somebody else laughed, short, and stopped.

Saul wrote with a pencil stub, because Culvert Nine's reader had been dead since the pumps went dry, and a dead reader keeps its records in graphite. Eleven cans. One blank rig. One stowaway. Pending review.

Miko didn't run. That was the part that got under Saul's skin; they could see it get there. The cord was two loops and a knot Miko could have had off in nine seconds, and she stood on the deck of a dead rig with her hand hanging and their eyes on that door like the door owed her money.

"She's not going anywhere," Saul said, to nobody.

"Nope," Miko said. "Your throat wants a matched crescent. I laid paper on it. Paper seals nothing, I know that now, I'm not stupid, I'm bored. So the only number in this yard that can open that door is standing behind it."

"Rule thirteen," Saul said. "Unlogged rig, unsealed load, no manifest. Seize it."

"Sure." Miko watched the slot at knee height. "Seize it and haul it four hours north on a rail with a cooked bearing, and hand a review officer eleven cans of frozen protein and a note that says a kid asked twice."

The bearing ticked as it cooled. The forward collar took its next bite, and the pitch came off it flat and final-sounding.

"That's four," Miko said.

Saul's pencil stopped.

Inside, something heavy shifted. Then a bolt drew back, three of them, one after another, unhurried, like somebody who had done it a thousand times and never once in a hurry. A pin dropped into the floor. Cold air came out through the gap in a slab, carrying chalk dust and the smell of grain sacks, and the storeroom door swung wide open.

The light behind the door was warmer than the yard, yellow and dense with dust, and it spilled out across the ties in a slab that caught the child first — small, hollow-cheeked, fingers knotted in the hem of a coat that had seen three winters and a growth spurt. She didn't step into the light. She stood in the frame of it, one hand on the door jamb, the other holding a bowl that had once had a lid.

Odessa Brill came through behind her. No coat. Sleeves rolled to the elbows over arms that moved like she'd spent twenty years throwing fifty-kilo sacks into a hatch and catching the rebound. Her hair was pulled back with a piece of wire, and the chalk dust on her forehead was a streak she'd put there herself, counting. She didn't look at Saul. She didn't look at Kass. She walked the canister line.

Eleven cans. Warm steel, condenser frost still feathering the collars where the cold-cycle hadn't bitten through yet. Bay 4 Shift 2 stamps on every receiving ring, crescent die, chipped at the left horn — the same chip Kass had matched in the shop, the same chip Ospina held in a red-blinking ring at Kettering. Brill didn't need a reader. She ran a thumbnail over each stamp, slow, like she was reading Braille, and her lips moved with the count.

"One. Two. Three."

The child whispered something. Brill didn't turn. "Four. Five. Six."

Saul's clipboard hung loose in their hand. The pencil was still between their fingers, graphite smudged on the thumb. "Brill —"

"Seven. Eight. Nine."

The forward canister sat at the end of the line, its collar bitten four times. The gasket seat was visible now, a black ring swelling where the steel had cold-flowed into the groove. The pitch of the last bite had been flat, final. The can was sealed. No reader would open it. No key would turn it. Only a torch, and time, and the protein inside turning to air while you cut.

Brill stopped at the bitten hoop. She didn't touch it. She didn't need to. The stamp was there on the ring, chipped crescent, Bay 4 Shift 2, same as the other ten.

"Ten. Eleven."

She said it flat, like she was reading a waybill off a dock. "These are Anza's payment. Not stolen cargo."

The child's bowl scraped the door jamb. *Is it here.*

Brill didn't answer. She looked up the line at the blank rig, then down at the jaw plate with its empty crescent, then at Miko's corded wrist, then at Kass's bad leg propped on the rail. Her eyes were the color of the ore dust — gray, flat, no shine.

"Eleven cans," she said. "Eleven short strikes on Nour's card. Eleven names on my wall that didn't eat last week." She tilted her head at the storeroom. "Forty names. Three crosses. You want to tell me which one of those is stolen cargo, Saul?"

Saul's jaw worked. "Rule thirteen —"

"Is yours." Brill's voice didn't rise. "This throat is mine. The plate is blank because I didn't stamp it. The reader is dead because the pumps are dead. The cans are warm because Anza sent them warm. The stamps match because Nour struck them short to pay for the compressor part your reader logged priority on without a trade." She took a breath. "You seize this load, my crew eats chalk dust for another month. You walk it north, the cans freeze shut, and Kettering gets eleven blocks of protein they can't open without a torch they don't have."

"Pending review," Saul said.

"Review doesn't feed anybody." Brill's gaze shifted to Miko, then to the J. Renner ticket lying flat on the blank plate, edges curling in the cold. "The throat opens on a matched seal or not at all. You know that. I know that. The kid knows that." She jerked her chin at the child. "So either the seal matches, or the door closes, and we all wait for the thaw."

The wind off the ridge tasted like iron and old oil. The bearing on the dead rig ticked, cooling. Somewhere up the line, a ghost train horn sounded — long, low, not for them.

Brill wiped her thumbnail on her sleeve. "Trade. That's the only rule left."

Saul squared the clipboard on their forearm, which is what a person does when they've decided the argument is a form and the form belongs to them.

"Rule thirteen," they said. "Unlogged rig, unsealed load, no manifest. I don't need her name to be right. I need the load's to be wrong."

"You need a torch," Miko said.

"I need a rail north and four hours."

"You've got a bearing that cooked itself coming down off the ridge. You'll be pushing that thing by hand past the second culvert and telling the desk the cans got cold on the way." Miko lifted her corded wrist an inch, not offering it, just showing the loop. "Cut it or don't. I'm not going anywhere. There's a kid behind you with a bowl."

"Rule thirteen doesn't have a bowl in it."

"No," Brill said. "It has you in it. You ate out of that room in Second Month, Saul. Two scoops and a dried apple, and you didn't ask whose mark was on the sack."

Saul's jaw set. "That's not a seal."

"It's a count." Brill wiped her thumb on her sleeve again, the same gesture, a woman with one gesture left. "You people run a continent on counts and get offended when somebody keeps one in chalk."

Kass came off the jaw plate in three bad steps, boot dragging, and put Nour's tally card face-out on the deck beside the canister line where the light fell. Card, not paper — a stiff strip of plate stock, punched at the top, eleven notches scratched down the left edge in four groups.

"I've got no authority here," Kass said. "I've got a leg with opinions and this." They turned the card with one finger so the receiving mark sat under the light: a crescent cut by hand, three strokes, C9 tucked in the hollow of it. "Eleven seals short, four down-line runs, all struck Bay 4 Shift 2. Same receiving mark every time. I've had this card since the bell at Anza and I've been carrying it around like an idiot looking for the hand that cut it."

Brill didn't reach for the card. She looked at it a long moment, the way you look at your own handwriting on something you don't remember writing.

"That's my hand," she said.

"Chalk," Saul said.

"Steel." Kass tapped the nearest receiving ring, the chipped crescent. "Her mark on the card, Nour's short strikes in the middle, your cans at the end. That's not stolen cargo, that's a debt with the ends tied. Your dead reader logged a compressor priority off this yard at oh-six-hundred, which is the only honest thing it's done since the pumps went dry. Somebody up the line is breathing on that compressor."

"Somebody up the line," Saul said, "is not in my rule."

Second collar took its first bite. The sound came off it clean and high, and everybody heard it.

"Ten cans left cycling," Miko said. "Forty seconds a bite, four bites a can, and it works down the line at its own pace, not ours. Call it nine minutes before the last one cures shut. Then it's a torch and a week, and the kid's still holding the bowl."

The child had come one step past the jamb. Just one. Brill put a hand back without looking and the child stopped, and didn't go in.

"Two of you have a claim on this jaw," Brill said. "One's got a rule and one's got a throat. Both of you can stand there and be right at each other till the steel's cold, and I'll tell you now how that ends, because I've watched it end twice. The cans go north frozen. My forty count chalk through Second Month. And the two of you write it up clean and go home to a node that eats."

"So open the throat," Saul said.

"I don't open it for a rule. I don't open it for a card, or a leg, or a name that isn't hers." Brill's voice stayed flat and low, and it carried anyway, out past the ties to the dead spur where the blank rig sat with its lamp bracket empty. "The throat opens on a matched seal or it doesn't open. And there's no seal in this yard tonight — so it opens on a trade."

She let that sit.

"That's the price. The whole of it. Nothing else moves that door."

PASSAGE ends.

Brill didn't look at the ticket on the plate. She didn't look at Saul's clipboard or Kass's card or Miko's corded wrist. She looked at the storeroom door, where the child still stood with the bowl, and the crew behind her — three women and a man, all of them lean in the way that comes from counting meals, not calories.

"One coast ticket," Brill said. "Buys unload rights. Eleven cans come in warm. My crew eats. The run logs under my name, and the skim-fault becomes mine to carry. I'll take no labor, no promise, no paper. The ticket or the door stays shut."

Saul's pencil moved. "A ticket is no seal. The reader logged the load pending review at oh-six-fourteen. That's a desk entry, not a throat entry. You don't overwrite a desk entry with a coast pass."

"I don't overwrite it. I *am* the throat." Brill turned, and the light caught the wire in her hair, the chalk streak on her forehead. "My storeroom. My plate. My rule. The reader's dead, Saul. The desk's four hours north and eating its own dust. The only seal that matters here is the one I say opens this door."

"That's not how the line works."

"Then the line doesn't work here." She took a step toward him, not threatening, not yielding. The crew behind her shifted — one woman's hand went to a wrench on her belt, the man's jaw set. "You ate out of this room. You know the count. You know what happens when the count stops. Get off my plate."

Saul's clipboard didn't move. "Rule thirteen —"

"Is yours. Not mine." Brill's voice was flat, final. "This is Culvert Nine. My name's on the wall. Forty names. Three crosses. You want to add a fourth, you tell me which one. Otherwise, you take your rule and your cord and your pending review, and you walk back up the ridge to whatever node sent you. The throat opens for a trade. That's the rule tonight. Take it or leave it."

The wind off the ridge carried the ghost train horn again, closer this time. The second canister's collar took its second bite, a clean high tick that cut through the silence.

Miko's thumb brushed the edge of the second ticket in her coat pocket. She didn't pull it out. She watched Brill's face, the way the wire held her hair, the chalk streak, the arms that had thrown sacks for twenty years.

Kass shifted weight onto their good leg, the bad one dragging in the gravel. "Brill —"

"Not now," Brill said, not looking at them. "The ticket. Or the door."

Saul stood on the jaw plate, clipboard raised, pencil poised. The reclamation cord ran from their hand to Miko's wrist, slack now, the knot tested and holding. Behind them, the blank rig sat in the dead spur with its lamp bracket empty, eleven cans breathing frost into the cold, ten still cycling, one already sealed shut.

"Your call," Saul said. "But the sheet goes north with M. Varel on it at the bell. That's not my rule. That's the line."

Brill didn't answer. She stood in the yellow slab of storeroom light, the child at her elbow, the crew at her back, and waited.

Saul's pencil didn't move. The clipboard stayed squared on their forearm, but something in the set of their shoulders went slack, the way a cable goes slack when the load shifts and the winch isn't taking it anymore.

"Right," they said. "Your throat. Your rule."

They reached for the knife at their belt — not the seal knife, the other one, the utility blade with the scored handle — and leaned over the rail. The cord came free in one clean draw, the loops falling slack around Miko's wrist. Miko didn't rub the mark. She didn't move.

"Load stands," Saul said, straightening. "Eleven cans, warm, matched stamps. Culvert Nine takes the delivery. Run logs under Brill. Skim-fault's yours to carry, you said. Fine. It's yours."

Brill didn't nod. She didn't relax. The child's bowl scraped the jamb again, quieter this time.

"But the sheet," Saul said. "M. Varel, stowaway-thief, unlogged rider on an unclaimed rig. That sheet goes north at the bell. That's not my rule and it's not your throat. That's the line. Unless a clean name answers for her before the tally closes."

Miko's fingers twitched at her coat pocket. Two tickets left. J. Renner and another, bought name, bought passage, bought silence.

"Clean name," she said. "Like the one on the ticket?"

"Like a name the desk accepts," Saul said. "Badge. Plate. Countersign. Something that holds up when the review officer turns the page. You've got until the bell."

The wind shifted. Up the ridge, past the dead spur and the blank rig and the ten cans still cycling their slow death, a bell began to toll. Low. Iron. Eighteen hundred. The shift turnaround at Anza, carried on air that had traveled forty kilometers of cold rail.

Kass heard it first. Their head came up, bad leg forgotten for a second, and they were already calculating — pedal-rail, cooked bearing, forty kilometers, two hours if the bearing held, three if it didn't, four if they had to push.

"Bell's tolling," Kass said. "I turn around now or I don't make the roster."

Saul didn't look at them. "Your turnaround's your problem. The sheet's mine. M. Varel rides north at the bell unless somebody puts a real name on it."

"Then put one on it," Miko said.

Saul's knife folded back into its sheath with a click that sounded final. "Not my name. Not my badge. Not my problem. I'm a reclamation agent. I seize what the rules say seize, and I write what the rules say write. You want the sheet clean, you bring me a name that holds water at Kettering. Before the bell."

They turned toward the pedal-rail where it sat chained to the jaw plate, bearing housing dark with old grease, Kass's chalk mark still on the frame: PR-ANZA-03 LIVE CULVERT NINE.

"Coming?" Saul called back. "Or you staying for the count?"

Kass was already moving, limping toward the rail, hands finding the release catch on the chain. The bell kept tolling, each stroke slower than the last, carrying the weight of a shift change four hours north and a node that would eat or not eat depending on what happened in the next nine minutes.

Miko stood in the yellow slab of light. The child watched. Brill watched. The crew behind Brill watched. Ten cans ticking. One sealed. Two tickets in a coat pocket. A name on a sheet that would ride north in the time it took a bell to finish tolling.
